card.hook: Picture a short climb up some stairs and then, boom, a whole rainforest rolling out below you, with green ridges fading into haze like a watercolour. Torre Yokahú is the easy way to get that view.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top of Torre Yokahú, the tower beside the road off PR-191 (there's a parking area close by). Face out over the rainforest canopy toward the mountains, and the coast and ocean if the day is clear.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of canopy, ridges and sky. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single peak, a misty ridge or a stretch of coast.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the green hills, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Aim for sunrise or sunset at the tower. A clear morning is your best bet, because cloud and mist often hide the high points.
card.selfie_here: Try the paved pull-off across from La Coca Falls on PR-191, near the park entrance. Use the front camera, stand with the falls behind you, and switch to 0.5x so the 85-foot fall squeezes in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the Yokahú Tower parking lot, about half a mile past La Coca Falls, to stand back so the tower fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay behind the roadside barrier at La Coca Falls, as the rocks can be wet and slippery if you go beyond it. Some trails and viewpoints may close or change, so check the official site for trail status before you go.
card.challenge: Can you catch three layers of green ridges, each one hazier than the last, in a single shot?
card.good_to_know: El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System, and the U.S. Forest Service has managed it since 1903. The Spanish Crown had already set the land aside in 1876 to protect its soil and water, which makes it one of the oldest forest reserves in the Western Hemisphere.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top of Torre Yokahú, the tower beside the road off PR-191 (there's a parking area close by). Face out over the rainforest canopy toward the mountains, and the coast and ocean if the day is clear.

card.hook: White water, dark rock and leaves crowding in from every side: La Coca Falls is a rainforest postcard, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 50 m north of the subject, near PR-191, at the phone icon on the map. Face south and the falls are right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and switch on the gridlines. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the forest around the falls, or 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out just the stream of water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white water, then slide it a touch darker so the falls keep their detail instead of turning into a blank patch.
card.best_time: Soft, even light is your friend, so an overcast spell or a moment when the falls are in shade works well. Harsh sun can leave bright patches on the water.
card.selfie_here: Take the path just left of the bridge down to the bottom of the falls, then scramble up a few rocks until you're right beside the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the cascade fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the roadside viewing area beside PR-191, facing the falls, so the whole cascade ends up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Rocks near the falls can be very slippery, so take it slowly. The rock-climbing spots are informal and unofficial, and access can change, so check the official El Yunque site before you go.
card.challenge: Put the main drop on a gridline, leave a few leaves in the corner of the frame, then shoot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x and pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: La Coca Falls sits inside El Yunque, where water, rock and thick green leaves all fit in one frame. Spray and humidity can fog your camera glass, so give it a quick wipe first. Access rules and path conditions can change, so check the official site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 50 m north of the subject, near PR-191, at the phone icon on the map. Face south and the falls are right in front of you.

card.hook: Two towers watch over El Yunque, and one of them is usually hiding in a cloud. Yokahú is the easier, friendlier one, and most people think it has the better view too.
card.stand_here: Stand near Torre de Yokahú, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Step back a little if there's room, then face the tower and tilt your phone up to fit in the full height.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole tower in from close range. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. If you climb up, try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out ridges and treetops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up one straight edge of the tower with a vertical line, then tap the tower and slide a bit darker if the sky starts going white.
card.best_time: Pick a clear spell, because cloud can hide the distance fast. Check the weather before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Try the stairs at the base of Yokahú Tower, which one visitor called a popular photo spot with the tower in frame. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and tilt up so the tower rises over your shoulder. It's not clear which step works best, so wander up and down until it looks right.
card.ask_someone: In the car park off PR-191, hand your phone to a friendly passer-by and ask them to shoot with you in the foreground and the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access and any rules about climbing the tower can change, so check the official El Yunque National Forest site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the tower stands perfectly straight against the sky, with a little sky left above the top. Can you do it without it leaning like it's had a long day?
card.good_to_know: Yokahú Tower was built in 1963 by Frank H. Wadsworth, who was then Forest Supervisor and Director of the IITF. It stands 69 feet (21 metres) tall, about 1,575 feet (480 m) above sea level. It's one of only two observation towers in the forest, and there's a car park close by.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Torre de Yokahú, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Step back a little if there's room, then face the tower and tilt your phone up to fit in the full height.

card.hook: Imagine a waterfall tumbling over dark boulders into a rocky pool, with green forest piled up on every side. La Mina Falls fits the water, the stone and the leaves into one frame, so your photo almost takes itself.
card.stand_here: Head for the pool-edge rocks at the base of La Mina Falls (Cascada La Mina), further on, to the east. Stand there facing straight into the falls, so the water drops over the boulders and fills your screen. Pick a firm, flat rock and keep your feet steady.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fill the frame with the falls. If the pool is too tight to step back, try zoom 0.5x. From the bridge, zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) picks the falls out from the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the main drop on one of the vertical lines with the pool along the bottom, then tap the brightest part of the falls and slide it a little darker so the white water keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning to noon is lovely, when the light filters through the leaves. Arriving early also helps you dodge the crowds for a cleaner, people-free shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the rocks leading down to the pool at the foot of the falls, which puts the waterfall right behind you. Switch to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the falls rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the bridge joining La Mina Trail and Big Tree Trail while you stand on the rocks below at the pool.
card.rules_and_safety: Please check first: recent reports say La Mina Trail and Big Tree Trail are closed for post-hurricane construction, so look at the US Forest Service notices on the day and don't go around barriers or try to reach the water if it's closed. If it's open, wear water shoes, since the rocks are slippery and there can be big drop-offs on the way down. Take care after rain because flash floods are a risk, and keep your phone in a pocket or zipped bag while you scramble, taking it out once you're standing safely.
card.challenge: Can you get the white water, the dark stone and the green forest all in one shot, with the main drop sitting neatly on a gridline?
card.good_to_know: La Mina Falls is on the Río de la Mina, deep in the forest of El Yunque. The trailhead is the ranger station at Palo Colorado (Km 12.2, Road 191). One walker's tip is to turn left just before the little bridge and make your way down to the water, and the bridge itself gives a calmer view of the falls from above, framed by trees.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the pool-edge rocks at the base of La Mina Falls (Cascada La Mina), further on, to the east. Stand there facing straight into the falls, so the water drops over the boulders and fills your screen. Pick a firm, flat rock and keep your feet steady.

card.hook: Picture a little stone tower with a pointy hat, popping out of a jungle of palms and wearing orange lichen like a knitted sweater. It looks almost fake against all that green, and that's why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand at the base of Mount Britton Tower in the summit clearing. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the tower so the conical roof sits above you among the palms and trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and fit the whole tower in with the trees around it. If it won't fit, tap 0.5x, but keep the tower in the middle of the frame so it doesn't stretch at the edges. Then step closer and try zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the stone and lichen.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the walls stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go early, because clouds often cover the summit and an early start gives you a better shot at a clear background. Mist can look lovely around the trees, but the sky may come out plain white.
card.selfie_here: Try the paved path just below the tower, with the stone facade behind you. We haven't confirmed this spot, so have a quick look when you get there. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and tap 0.5x if your phone has it so the tower sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The trail can be slippery, especially on the way down in rain or cloud. Access can change, so check the El Yunque National Forest alerts on the day, as the road or tower may be closed or reservation rules may have changed.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one of the whole tower in its green frame, and one of the orangest patch of lichen you can find. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Mount Britton Tower is a small stone tower with a conical roof, standing in a summit clearing in El Yunque. It's free to visit, but you walk up the Mount Britton Trail, about 0.8 miles one way with some steep sections, so take water. The top of the tower is a viewpoint rather than a place to photograph the tower itself, so shoot it from the ground.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the base of Mount Britton Tower in the summit clearing. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the tower so the conical roof sits above you among the palms and trees.

card.hook: You hike uphill through the rainforest, reach the top, and the sky is a big blank grey. Welcome to El Yunque, where the mist is half the charm and the other half is hoping it lifts.
card.stand_here: Stand at Mt. Britton Tower, at the top of the Mt. Britton trail. Face north-east, because the peak is about 800 m to the north-east as the crow flies.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big view over the forest and coast. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the peak. Switch to 0.5x if you want the tower rail and the forest in the same shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the forest, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the bright mist doesn't turn everything grey.
card.best_time: Go on a clear morning, because cloud and mist often hide the summit later in the day. Take a first shot the moment you reach the tower, since the cloud can close in fast, then wait a few minutes and shoot again if the mist lifts.
card.selfie_here: Head to the top level of Yokahú Tower and turn your back on the forest canopy and the ocean. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and expect a possible queue.
card.ask_someone: At the La Coca Falls parking area beside PR-191, ask someone to shoot from the parking side so the full 85-foot falls fit in the frame, while you pose in front of the falls.
card.rules_and_safety: The rocks below La Coca Falls can be slippery, so take care when posing near them. Parts of the El Yunque trails have been closed in recent years, so check the official site and the current trail status before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the peak peeking out of the mist, then take a second shot when the cloud rolls back in and spot the difference.
card.good_to_know: The Taíno called this mountain Yukiyu. It stands just over 1,000 metres tall and is the second-highest peak in the forest after El Toro. The forest is also the rainiest of all US national forests, so a misty peak is normal.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Mt. Britton Tower, at the top of the Mt. Britton trail. Face north-east, because the peak is about 800 m to the north-east as the crow flies.

card.hook: Here's a swimming pool where the only thing you're allowed to dive into is your camera roll. Baño Grande is a 1930s stone pool with a waterfall spilling over its dam, and it looks great in photos.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stone staircase that climbs up to the pool. The phone icon on the map is right on it. Climb a few steps, then turn around and look back so the man-made falls pour over the dam in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x on the staircase so you get the steps, the falls and the forest together. At the top, try 0.5x to squeeze the whole stonework and pool into one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the falls on one line with a few stone steps at the bottom of the frame, then tap the falls and slide darker a touch so the white water keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft, even light under cloud or in the shade is best for water and wet stone. It's rainforest, so check the weather first. The site is open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the stone steps climbing up from the Palo Colorado side, where the falls over the dam are in view, and tuck them behind your shoulder. The arched stone bridge at the upstream end of the pool is another good spot, but check the framing on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the roadside across Highway 191 from the Palo Colorado Information Center, facing the pool and dam, while you pose on the pool side of the road.
card.rules_and_safety: No swimming is allowed, so keep to the stone paths and stay out of the water. The steps can be slippery, so take care, especially near the edges. Check current access with the National Forest before you set off.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the falls on a gridline and the steps leading your eye up, then a second with the pool framed by stonework and trees.
card.good_to_know: Baño Grande was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps between 1935 and 1938 and was used until 1968, when it closed for safety reasons. It's about 5.5 metres deep and roughly three times the size of the nearby Baño de Oro. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the stone staircase that climbs up to the pool. The phone icon on the map is right on it. Climb a few steps, then turn around and look back so the man-made falls pour over the dam in front of you.
